nodes.name: Hydrothermal Synthesis and Calcination
nodes.procedure: A simple one-step hydrothermal method was used to synthesize α-, β- and δ-MnO₂, respectively. Three MnO₂ catalysts with different crystal structures were prepared by adjusting the molar ratios of KMnO₄ and MnSO₄·H₂O (n_KMnO4 : n_MnSO4·H₂O = 2.5, 0.5, and 5.5) and then maintaining them at different reaction temperatures for 12 h. The obtained catalysts were calcined in an air atmosphere at 360°C for 2 h with a heating rate of 5°C·min⁻¹. Subsequently, α-, β-, and δ-MnO₂ electrodes were fabricated on a carbon paper substrate.

The obtained catalysts were calcined in an air atmosphere at 360°C for 2 h with a heating rate of 5°C·min⁻¹.

nodes.characterization_summary: TXRD confirms successful synthesis of α-MnO2 (JCPDS 44-0141, cryptomelane), β-MnO2 (JCPDS 24-0735, pyrolusite), and δ-MnO2 (JCPDS 80-1098, birnessite) with α- and β-MnO2 showing sharp narrow peaks indicating better crystallinity while δ-MnO2 exhibits broad bands and lower crystallinity.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The TXRD results (Figure 1a) confirm the successful synthesis of α-, β-, and δ-MnO₂ catalysts, according to JCPDS 44-0141 (cryptomelane), JCPDS 24-0735 (pyrolusite), and JCPDS 80-1098 (birnessite), respectively.

properties.description: X-ray diffraction pattern of MnO2 samples

nodes.characterization_summary: SEM shows α-MnO2 with stacking-nanoneedle structure (35 nm thickness), β-MnO2 with coarser shorter nanorods, and δ-MnO2 as polymerized flower-like nanosheets (10 nm thickness).
nodes.evidence_snippet: The SEM image of α-MnO₂ (Figure 1b) presented a stacking-nanoneedle structure with a thickness of about 35 nm.

nodes.characterization_summary: HRTEM of α-MnO2 shows lattice spacings of 0.152 nm (521), 0.239 nm (211), 0.181 nm (411); β-MnO2 shows 0.311 nm (110); δ-MnO2 shows 0.218 nm (-112), 0.225 nm (201), confirming poor crystallinity of δ-MnO2.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Clear lattice stripes were observed in the HRTEM (Figure 1e), and the crystal plane spacing of 0.152 nm, 0.239 nm, and 0.181 nm corresponded to the α-MnO₂ (521), (211), and (411) planes, respectively.

nodes.characterization_summary: XPS shows K+ in α- and δ-MnO2 tunnels but not in β-MnO2; Mn 2p3/2 peaks at 642.7 eV (Mn4+), 641.7 eV (Mn3+), 640.6 eV (Mn2+) with low-valence Mn content order α-MnO2 > δ-MnO2 > β-MnO2; O 1s shows α-MnO2 with highest Oads proportion.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Figure 2b shows the XPS spectra of Mn 2p3/2 for MnO₂, and the peaks at 642.7 eV, 641.7 eV, and 640.6 eV could be attributed to Mn4+, Mn3+, and Mn2+, respectively.

nodes.characterization_summary: Raman band shifts at 630.8 cm⁻¹ (α-MnO2), 629.3 cm⁻¹ (β-MnO2), 621.8 cm⁻¹ (δ-MnO2) ascribed to enhanced symmetric stretching vibration related to oxygen vacancies.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The Raman spectrum in Figure 2d demonstrated that the band shifts of α-, β-, and δ-MnO₂ are at 630.8, 629.3, and 621.8 cm⁻¹.

nodes.characterization_summary: CV curves at scan rates 10-100 mV/s used to calculate ECSA, with α-MnO2 showing steeper slopes indicating larger ECSA and higher activity than β-MnO2 and δ-MnO2.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The electrochemically active surface area (ECSA) indicated the effective area of the electrode involved in the catalytic reaction, which was calculated and fitted by the CV curves of the catalysts at different scanning rates (Figure S3).

nodes.characterization_summary: EIS Nyquist plots show α-MnO2 has smallest curve radius indicating lowest charge-transfer impedance and fastest electron-transfer rate.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The curve radius of α-MnO₂ was the smallest, indicating that it had a lower charge-transfer impedance and faster electron-transfer rate.
